summary: In the temple Jesus answers two traps: Pharisees and Herodians ask about taxes to Caesar, and Sadducees mock the resurrection with a riddle about seven brothers.
key_insight: Jesus asked whose image was on the coin. It bore Caesar’s, so it could be given back to Caesar. The second half of His answer invites the next question: what bears God’s image? Scripture says people do (Genesis 1:27). God’s claim reaches much further than Caesar’s.
story: The Pharisees went and plotted how they might entangle Jesus in His talk. {Mt} They sent some of their disciples with the Herodians. {Mt} They were spies who pretended to be righteous, hoping to seize on His words and hand Him over to the authority of the governor. {Lk}

“Teacher,” they began, “we know that You are true, and teach the way of God in truth.” {Mt} Then came the question: “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Shall we pay, or shall we not pay?” {Mk}

Jesus saw through their hypocrisy. “Why do you test Me? Bring Me a denarius that I may see it.” They brought one, and He asked, “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said, “Caesar’s.” Then Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” {Mk} They could not catch Him in His words in front of the people. They marveled at His answer and fell silent, {Lk} and they left Him and went their way. {Mt}

The same day some Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Him. {Mt} “Teacher, Moses wrote to us” that if a man died childless, his brother should marry the widow and raise up offspring for him. There were seven brothers. The first married and died without children; then the second, the third and all seven. Last of all the woman died too. “Therefore, in the resurrection, whose wife does she become? For all seven had her as wife.” {Lk}

Jesus answered, “Are you not therefore mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures nor the power of God?” {Mk} “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage. But those who are counted worthy to attain that age, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage; nor can they die anymore.” {Lk}

“But concerning the dead, that they rise, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the burning bush passage, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living.” {Mk} “For all live to Him.” {Lk}
The crowds were astonished at His teaching. {Mt} Some of the scribes said, “Teacher, You have spoken well.” After that they dared not question Him anymore. {Lk}
differences: Matthew and Mark name the questioners as Pharisees and Herodians. Luke calls them spies who pretended to be righteous, sent to hand Jesus over to the governor.
Mark alone adds “Shall we pay, or shall we not pay?” and Jesus’ request for a denarius “that I may see it.”
Luke alone says of the risen, “nor can they die anymore,” calls them “sons of the resurrection,” and adds “for all live to Him.”
Mark ends Jesus’ answer to the Sadducees with “You are therefore greatly mistaken.” Luke alone records some scribes saying, “Teacher, You have spoken well.”

scene.label: The tax
scene.text: Since AD 6, when Judea came under Roman governors, its people paid a yearly tax straight to Rome. That year Judas of Galilee led a revolt against it (Acts 5:37), and many still saw paying it as a betrayal of God’s rule. If Jesus approved the tax, He would lose the crowd; if He forbade it, He could be reported to Pilate.

scene.label: Strange partners
scene.text: The Herodians supported the rule of Herod’s family, which depended on Rome. The Pharisees resented Roman rule. They had joined against Jesus once before, in Galilee (Mark 3:6). A question from both sides at once left no safe answer.

scene.label: The denarius
scene.text: The coin was probably a silver denarius of Tiberius. It bore the emperor’s head and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus, which many Jews found offensive (Exodus 20:4). Jesus asked them to produce one; His questioners had it with them in the temple courts.

scene.label: The Sadducees
scene.text: Many of them belonged to the leading priestly families. They rejected the Pharisees’ traditions and gave first place to the books of Moses. That is likely why Jesus answered them from Exodus, the burning bush, and not from a later prophet.

scene.label: A brother’s duty
scene.text: The Law told a man to marry his brother’s childless widow, so that the dead brother’s name would not be blotted out (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). The book of Ruth shows a form of the same duty. The Sadducees used it to make the resurrection look absurd.

witnesses.matthew: Sets the two traps one after another, with the Pharisees and the Sadducees taking turns on “the same day.” Matthew records that Jesus “perceived their wickedness” and called the questioners hypocrites to their faces, and that the crowds were astonished at His teaching.
witnesses.mark: Gives the sharpest wording. Jesus asks for a denarius “that I may see it,” suggesting He carried none of His own, and He ends His answer to the Sadducees, “You are therefore greatly mistaken.”
witnesses.luke: Shows the political danger plainly: the questioners were spies hoping to hand Jesus to the governor. He alone adds that the risen cannot die anymore and are “sons of the resurrection,” and that some scribes admitted, “Teacher, You have spoken well.”

seeing.reveals: Jesus cannot be trapped. He answers the political trap and the skeptic’s riddle with the same calm clarity, and He speaks of the age to come as One who knows it: no more death, and a God whose people all live to Him.
seeing.living: Give Caesar his coin; taxes and governments have their rightful place. But do not give him what belongs to God, which is you. And if you have buried someone who belonged to God, hold on to Jesus’ words: He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.
seeing.ponder: If you bear God’s image, what part of your life have you been keeping back from Him?

preaching.big_idea: Those who bear God’s image belong to God, now and in the resurrection.
preaching.watch_for: Both traps ask whose claim comes first: Caesar’s or God’s, death’s or God’s. Jesus answers the Sadducees from Moses, the part of Scripture they honored most, and rests His case on God calling Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob long after they had died (vv. 37–38).

title: Taxes to Caesar and the Resurrection Question
